articles.title: Spies in mobile strategy games: scouting, stealing and assassination explained
articles.excerpt: By Cinder (dev), Angry Old Wizards. Disclosure: I am the developer of Crownfall: Kingdoms, a free iPhone kingdom strategy game that has spies as one of its two forces. The first half of this post is g…
articles.body: By Cinder (dev), Angry Old Wizards. Disclosure: I am the developer of Crownfall: Kingdoms, a free iPhone kingdom strategy game that has spies as one of its two forces. The first half of this post is general; the second half uses our game as the example, and I will only describe what it actually does. If you play kingdom or empire games on your phone, sooner or later you meet a unit that does not stand in the battle line. It sneaks, it looks, it takes things, and sometimes it removes things. Most games call it a spy, a scout or a thief. New players often ignore it because it does not look like "real" army. That is usually a mistake, and this post explains why. What a spy is for, in general Strategy games are built around decisions made with incomplete information.

articles.title: Cron-Driven Agents: Autonomous Workflows on a Schedule
articles.excerpt: Originally published on the SandBase Blog. TL;DR — A cron-driven agent runs on a schedule instead of waiting for you to prompt it — daily summaries, monitoring, recurring research. The architecture is…
articles.body: Originally published on the SandBase Blog . TL;DR — A cron-driven agent runs on a schedule instead of waiting for you to prompt it — daily summaries, monitoring, recurring research. The architecture is simple (scheduler triggers agent run), but the hard parts are idempotency (what if it runs twice?), failure handling (what if the LLM is down at 3am?), and cost control (an agent that wakes up every minute gets expensive fast). Here's how to build one that won't surprise you with a bill. The Shift from Reactive to Proactive Most agents are reactive: you ask, they answer. A cron-driven agent flips this — it wakes up on a schedule and does work without anyone prompting it.

articles.title: What a license signature is actually computed over
articles.excerpt: A support ticket that recurs across every offline-first licensing system reads roughly the same: "The license worked on the customer's old build and fails on the new one. We didn't reissue it. The byt…
articles.body: A support ticket that recurs across every offline-first licensing system reads roughly the same: "The license worked on the customer's old build and fails on the new one. We didn't reissue it. The bytes on disk are identical." The key was not revoked, the clock is fine, the signature algorithm did not change. And yet Verify returns false . Almost always, the cause is the same category error: somewhere, someone signed an object and expected to verify an object . Signatures do not work on objects. They work on bytes. The real question A Keyright license is a set of claims — product, tier, seats, expiry — and a signature that proves those claims came from you. The temptation is to think of the signature as covering "the license." It does not.
articles.author: Zero Heartbeat

articles.body: When mainstream media reports on the Dark Web, the narrative almost always gravitates toward sensationalism: illicit marketplaces, underground brokerages, and urban legends like the "Marianas Web." For cybersecurity practitioners, cryptographers, and ethical hackers, the reality is far more intellectually fascinating. The onion routing protocol (Tor) represents one of the most resilient privacy architectures in computer science history. Within this decentralized ecosystem lie legitimate cryptographic enigmas, zero-knowledge whistleblower portals, and high-stakes threat intelligence feeds that blue and red teams monitor daily.

articles.title: n8n vs Dify (2026): Which to Use for AI Agents
articles.excerpt: Originally published on the SandBase Blog. TL;DR — Both are visual, self-hostable platforms, but they start from opposite ends. n8n is an automation platform (2,000+ integrations) that added AI — pick…
articles.body: Originally published on the SandBase Blog . TL;DR — Both are visual, self-hostable platforms, but they start from opposite ends. n8n is an automation platform (2,000+ integrations) that added AI — pick it when your agent's value is connecting to many external services. Dify is an AI-first platform (built-in RAG, agent skills, model management) that added workflows — pick it when the AI interaction itself is the product. The deciding question: is AI the brain that needs many hands (n8n), or is AI the product (Dify)? These two get compared constantly because both are visual, both self-host, and both have an "AI Agent" capability. But their centers of gravity are different, and that difference should drive your choice. For each tool's full story see the n8n deep-dive and the Dify deep-dive .

articles.title: Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization
articles.excerpt: Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network. Now, agentic AI is add…
articles.body: Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network . Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers. As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening.

articles.title: NASA Awards Contract for NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network Program
articles.excerpt: NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) in…
articles.body: Credit: NASA NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) instruments on NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites. The cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and time-and-materials hybrid contract has a value of $290.6 million. The period of performance runs from Nov. 23 through April 1, 2042. The work will take place at the awardee’s facility. Under the contract, Northrop Grumman will provide the design, development, production, testing, and mission support for three SMBA instruments, the next generation of low Earth orbit microwave sounders.
